title: The rasa dance
hookLine: a full moon, a flute, a circle dance, and a God who disappears the moment anyone feels special
carry: pride hides God; longing brings him back

lines: A FULL MOON AND A FLUTE.
cards: An autumn night, the moon full over the Yamuna. Krishna plays his flute at the edge of the forest. In the village, the gopis hear it, and they drop everything.
One leaves the milk on the stove. One leaves a meal half served. One is halfway through putting on her makeup, one eye done.
They run to the forest. And the first thing Krishna says when they arrive is: why are you here? It's night.
Go home to your families. That's your duty.

teach.b: This is the rasa lila, from the tenth part of the Bhagavata Purana, and some devotees call it the heart of the whole book. The gopis won't go. We've left everything for you, they say.
Where would we go? So he stays, and walks and laughs with them in the moonlight. Then something happens in the gopis' hearts.
Each begins to feel proud, the best of women, singled out. In that moment, Krishna disappears. The gopis search the forest, asking the trees and the vines if they've seen him.
They act out his stories to feel close to him. They sing a song of longing, known as the Gopi Gita. When their pride is gone and only longing remains, he appears again.
Then comes the rasa dance itself: a great circle, and Krishna multiplies himself so that every gopi feels he is right beside her.
Devotees hear it as the love of souls for God, not an ordinary romance; the Bhagavata itself says it's God's play, not a pattern to imitate. Two teachings of bhakti stand out.
Pride hides God; longing brings him back.
And God is fully present to each person, not divided among them.

teach.h: A CIRCLE, AND HE'S BESIDE EACH ONE.
teach.b: That's why, when devotees sing Krishna's names together, nobody is meant to be the star.
And it lands today, too: the moment you feel like the chosen one, the best in the room, is the moment the story says God feels farthest.

teach.h: IN THE CIRCLE, EVERYONE IS CLOSEST.
teach.b: In the circle, everyone is closest.

how: The rasa lila is performed in dance and drama, especially in Vrindavan and in Manipuri and other classical dance, and Vaishnava devotees read the gopis' love as the highest model of devotion to God, not as a pattern for human behavior.

o: action, like running toward the flute
the pride that makes a person feel chosen
a duty to stay home with the family

games.q: the rasa night — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna first welcomes the gopis with open arms
he first tells them to go home to their families. they refuse.
Krishna disappears when the gopis grow proud
each feels she alone has won him, and he vanishes.
the Bhagavata says people should imitate the rasa lila
it says the story is God's play, not a pattern to imitate, and hearing it with faith frees from lust.

games.q: you're one of the gopis. Krishna has vanished from the forest. what do you do?
o: search the forest, asking the trees, and sing your longing.
wait angrily for him to apologize.
games.why: they search, act out his stories and sing. when pride is gone and only longing remains, he appears again.

practice: Notice any small pride in you right now, nothing dramatic, I'm doing well at this, I'm better than I was, and set it down gently, the way you'd put down a bag.

Then notice what's left underneath, a longing maybe, for peace, for closeness, for something you can't name, and breathe with it without trying to fix it. If you pray, you can let the longing itself be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and the gopis' action was running toward the flute, and letting go of pride once they got there.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the circle dance of Krishna and the gopis; lila means play. The rasa lila is told in Bhagavata 10.29–10.33.

carryVoice: Your line: pride hides God; longing brings him back. And in the circle, he's beside each one. Three hundred twelve days, and counting.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.29–10.33 (the rasa lila; the gopis' search; the Gopi Gita; the rasa dance; Parikshit's question)
